intro.title: Reading error messages
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Every programmer sees errors all day. They are not a sign you did badly; they are JavaScript telling you, as exactly as it can, what went wrong and where. Learning to read them is the fastest way to get unstuck.

An error message has two parts: the **type** of error, and a **message**. The editor also points at the **line** where it happened.

```
// This shows an error: run it and read the message
const price = 10
console.log(pirce * 2)
```

`ReferenceError: pirce is not defined` says the kind of problem (a name JavaScript doesn't know) and which name. The fix is often a typo.

The four you will meet most:

- **SyntaxError**: the code can't even be read, like a missing bracket or quote. Nothing runs at all.
- **ReferenceError**: a name that doesn't exist (a typo, or used before its `let`/`const`).
- **TypeError**: a value is the wrong kind for what you did, like calling something that isn't a function, or reading a property of `undefined`.
- **RangeError**: a value is out of the allowed range, like a function that calls itself forever.

```
// This shows an error: reading a property of undefined
const user = undefined
console.log(user.name)
```

The line pointed at is where JavaScript *noticed* the problem, which isn't always where the mistake *is*. Here the error is on the second line, but the real bug is that `user` was never given a value. Ask "where did this value come from?" and work backwards.

When code stops with an error, the lines after it don't run. Output before it is still shown, which helps you see how far it got.

intro.title: Debugging: finding bugs that don't crash
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The worst bugs give no error at all: the code runs, but the answer is wrong. Finding them is **debugging**, and it is a skill you can learn like any other.

Step one: know what you **expected**, and find the first place where reality is different. The simplest tool is `console.log`: show the values in the middle of the code and see where they stop making sense.

```
const prices = [4, 10, 6]
let total = 0
for (let i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) {
  console.log("adding", prices[i])
  total += prices[i]
}
console.log(total)
```

The log shows `adding 10` and `adding 6`, but never `adding 4`: the loop starts at 1, not 0. This is an **off-by-one** bug, one of the most common there is.

A checklist of usual suspects:

- **Off by one**: `<` vs `<=`, starting at 1 vs 0, `length` vs `length - 1`.
- **`=` vs `===`**: `if (x = 5)` *sets* `x` and is always true.
- **Text vs number**: `"5" + 1` is `"51"`. Values from input are text until you convert them.
- **The wrong variable**: updating `total` inside the loop but showing `sum`.
- **Changed when it shouldn't be**: `sort` and `push` change an array that other code still uses.
- **Missing `return`**: the function gives `undefined`.

Label your logs (`console.log("total after loop", total)`) so you know which is which, and log `typeof x` when the kind of value matters. Remove them when you're done.

When the code is long, cut the problem down: try the smallest input that still goes wrong, and test pieces on their own. Explaining the code line by line, even to nobody, finds a surprising number of bugs; programmers call it "rubber duck debugging".

intro.title: Missing values: ?. and ??
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The most common error of all is `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. It happens when you read into something that isn't there: a user with no address, a list item past the end, a setting nobody set.

**Optional chaining**, `?.`, reads a property only if the thing before it exists. If it is `null` or `undefined`, the whole expression gives `undefined` instead of an error:

```
const ana = { name: "Ana", address: { city: "Lima" } }
const ben = { name: "Ben" }

console.log(ana.address?.city)
console.log(ben.address?.city)
```

It works for indexes and calls too: `list?.[0]` and `user.greet?.()` (call it only if it exists).

Then **`??`** (the nullish coalescing operator) gives a fallback when a value is `null` or `undefined`:

```
const ben = { name: "Ben" }
console.log(ben.address?.city ?? "Unknown city")
```

Why `??` and not `||`? `||` falls back for *any* falsy value, including `0`, `""` and `false`, which are often real answers. `??` only falls back when the value is truly missing:

```
const settings = { volume: 0, nickname: "" }
console.log(settings.volume || 5, settings.volume ?? 5)
console.log(settings.nickname || "anon", settings.nickname ?? "anon")
```

`??=` sets a variable or property only if it is missing: `options.size ??= 10`.

Don't sprinkle `?.` everywhere. Use it where a value is *allowed* to be missing. If something should always be there, an error when it isn't tells you about a real bug.

intro.title: Medium side quest: A form validator
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A sign-up form has fields for a name, an email, an age and a password. When someone presses "Sign up", the app should list **every** problem at once, next to the field it belongs to, rather than one at a time.

Build it from small **rules**. A rule is a function that takes a value and returns an error message, or `null` if the value is fine:

```
const required = (value) => (String(value ?? "").trim() === "" ? "This field is required" : null)
console.log(required(""), required("Kim"))
```

Each field has a list of rules. `validate(form, rules)` runs them all and returns `{ ok, errors }`, where `errors` has the first problem for each field:

```text
{ ok: false, errors: { email: "Email looks wrong", age: "Must be at least 13" } }
```

Finally, rule **factories** like `minLength(8)` make rules with settings, using a closure.
